title: 316L skid fabrication and orbital welding, ASME BPE | Aquemi
meta: 316L skids and loops built to ASME BPE: EN 10204 3.1 heat traceability, ASME IX welders, weld maps, borescope records, ASTM A967 passivation, CRN vessels.
headline: Fabrication your auditor can trace from any weld back to the mill heat
lead: We build 316L skids, tanks and loops to ASME BPE with orbital welds. Every product-contact weld is numbered and logged with its operator, procedure, coupon, inspection and EN 10204 3.1 heat numbers.
primary_cta_intent: Review of a document you have|Fabrication or piping specification

blocks.h: Weld evidence is made at the bench, or lost
body: Weld evidence is made at the bench or not at all: an insulated weld cannot be re-inspected, and a cut tube loses its heat number. EU GMP Annex 15, 3.9 expects installation qualification (IQ) to check materials against the approved drawings.
Audit findings are rarely bad welds. They are missing inspection records, certificates that do not match the heats installed, and coupons never kept.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Our specification says 3.1B certificates. Do you supply those?
items.a: 3.1B is the 1991 EN 10204 designation. The 2004 edition replaced it with 3.1: specific test results, validated by an inspection representative independent of manufacturing. We supply 3.1 and note the equivalence in the material log. A type 2.2 test report is not accepted for product-contact parts.

items.q: How do you tie 3.1 certificates to the tube and fittings?
items.a: Heat numbers are checked against the certificate on receipt and [how components are marked or tagged]. Each weld log line names the heat numbers on both sides, so any weld traces back to its certificates.

Our standard is [share of product-contact welds borescoped, %] of product-contact welds, stated in the plan before work starts. ASME BPE allows a random sample; most pharmaceutical owners specify more. A weld that cannot be reached, such as a final closure, is accepted on its coupon and the reason logged.

items.q: What happens to a rejected weld?
items.a: It is cut out, not ground or re-fused. The replacement gets a new number, its own log line and inspection, and the log keeps the link to the rejected weld. Rejection rate in the dossier: [weld rejection rate reported, yes or no].

items.q: Can we audit the shop and see a real weld log?
items.a: Yes to audits and witnessing. Hold and witness points are agreed in the plan, typically coupons, borescope review, pressure test and passivation. Shop: [shop location, city and province]. Sample log: [redacted weld log shareable under NDA, yes or no]. See quality management.

items.q: Do we need electropolish, and who passivates?
items.a: Not by rule. SF1 is common for Purified Water (PW); we recommend SF4 for hot WFI, pure steam and tank interiors, where rouge is more likely. Welds made after electropolishing are passivated. Done by: [in-house or named subcontractor]. The certificate names standard, chemistry, temperature, contact time and verification test.

Vessels are designed to ASME Section VIII, Division 1 and registered under CSA B51 in the province of installation, which issues the CRN. Fabricator: [ASME certificate holder or certified vessel partner]. Registered in: [provinces where Aquemi registers]. Fittings and, in some provinces, piping also need registration; we confirm at design.

Built by: [panel shop and certification mark held]. The marks that apply are CSA C22.2 No. 286 for Canada or UL 508A for US installations. An uncertified panel can be stopped at site by the electrical inspector, so we settle this before order.
